players.product: Large-scale liquid-cooled AI data-center campuses (Polaris Forge / Delta Forge)

quarterly_data.signal: CEO Wes Cummins: Applied Digital signed leases for five campuses over the year, three of them in the past four months, creating $36 billion of total contracted long-term lease value with approximately $20 billion of that in the last quarter - a 125% increase in contracted lease value, underpinned by 1.41 GW of contracted critical IT load. Since the call a year earlier it went from one campus to five, increased contracted revenue from $7 billion-$36 billion and added over a gigawatt of capacity with investment-grade customers, with over 80% of that leased to a high investment-grade customer. After signing CoreWeave first, the company committed to reach 70% of contracted lease revenue through investment-grade hyperscalers; the CEO says it is now at 76% and will soon be close to 80%. CEO: 'we have about two plus billion of net operating income contracted on an annual basis'. Five multi-billion dollar AI factory campuses are under construction for three separate hyperscalers, and the CEO says all construction projects are on time and on budget.
quarterly_data.figure: $36 billion contracted lease value (125% increase), approximately $20 billion in the last quarter; 1.41 GW contracted critical IT load; 76% investment grade

capex.display: $36 billion of total contracted long-term lease value

quarterly_data.signal: Pipeline beyond the 1.41 GW under construction: CEO says rental rates 'have moved higher over the past six months'; Applied Digital is actively marketing an additional 1.7 GW across multiple states, expects it to command higher pricing, and expects that capacity to go to new customers. It is in advanced negotiations with two existing investment-grade customers on expansion options of approximately 100 MW and 150 MW: at Polaris Forge 2 it started two buildings (300 MW) and contracted 200 MW, and expects 'in the near term' to contract the additional 100 MW with the same tenant; at one of the Delta Forge campuses it is negotiating a third building with the tenant. Management expects these expansions on substantially the same terms as the current leases but at materially higher lease rates and possibly longer duration; if executed they would bring total capacity to 1.66 GW and add over $6 billion of contracted revenue at existing rates and duration (CEO expects the ultimate amount to be greater). CEO: expansion on current campuses alone gives visibility to over five gigawatts of critical IT load through 2032, and the company expects to keep adding new campuses this year and next.
quarterly_data.figure: 1.7 GW marketed; approximately 100 MW and 150 MW expansions in advanced negotiation; 1.66 GW and over $6 billion additional contracted revenue if executed; over 5 GW visibility through 2032

quarterly_data.signal: Outlook: CEO - a year ago the company set a goal of $1 billion of net operating income within five years; it now expects to achieve that run-rate goal a year from now, three years ahead of schedule. CFO Saidal Mohmand: capex should be 'around $600 million-ish for the upcoming quarter' and will step up as construction at the new campuses reaches more advanced stages. The company is building towards 1.5 GW of HPC AI infrastructure and expects the ramp to drive meaningful growth in revenue, EBITDA and NOI; current HPC financials reflect mainly the initial 100 MW online during the quarter, and investors should expect 'a significant step-up in our numbers over the coming quarters and years'. CFO on NOI margin: the company aims conservative on margin targets; margins should rise after a site's initial RFS as operations improve and with economies of scale as more buildings are added on a campus, on a timeline that may differ by region.
quarterly_data.figure: $1 billion NOI run-rate goal expected a year from now (three years ahead of schedule); capex around $600 million for the upcoming quarter; building towards 1.5 GW

quarterly_data.signal: Fiscal Q4 detail from the CFO: net operating income (HPC base rental revenue less rental operating expenses, property taxes and insurance) was $39.9 million, a 91% margin; adjusted EBITDA $42.4 million, up from $1 million in the comparative prior quarter; net loss attributable to common shareholders $111.6 million or $0.39 per share. Data center rental and other cost of revenues of $25.1 million included approximately $14.1 million of depreciation and amortization for the first HPC data center at Polaris Forge 1. The Data Center Hosting segment (energized space for Bitcoin mining at two North Dakota sites) generated $37.3 million of revenue and $12.5 million of segment operating profit on $113.8 million in reported assets; CEO: it is paid on capacity provided regardless of the Bitcoin price and remains the highest return-on-asset business in the portfolio. Stock-based compensation included $47.9 million of one-time awards tied to the ChronoScale transaction and $65.1 million tied to performance stock units. Quarter end: $4.2 billion in cash, $5 billion in debt and approximately $1.7 billion in equity.
quarterly_data.figure: NOI $39.9 million (91% margin); adjusted EBITDA $42.4 million; Data Center Hosting $37.3 million revenue, $12.5 million segment operating profit

quarterly_data.signal: Constraints and execution: CEO says managing supply chain and power are 'probably the two biggest constraints at the moment'. Applied Digital has contracted 2.1 GW of utility power over the past year and times building starts to when power becomes available. On supply chain, it locked in large mechanical, electrical and plumbing capacity a few years ago - about 700 MW per year of critical IT load - and has contracted to build 1.5 GW over the next couple of years, 'definitely exceeding that a little bit'; it has kept expanding that limit. Construction pace: the first Polaris Forge 1 building took about 24 months from start of construction to RFS, the second under 12 months. It previously said it could work on seven campuses simultaneously (five today); the CEO thinks it can go higher but does not want to overextend. Labor rates have been fairly steady over the past six months; the company avoids crowded markets (the CEO says it is the only one really building in North Dakota) and trains workers with local technical and vocational colleges. New-campus builds run toward the high end of its cost band because the first buildings carry all campus costs (new substations and on-campus transmission, land, the power site); one southern site will be slightly higher because of additional dirt work and site prep.
quarterly_data.figure: 2.1 GW utility power contracted over the past year; about 700 MW per year supply chain capacity vs 1.5 GW contracted to build; about 24 months to RFS for the first building, under 12 months for the second

quarterly_data.signal: Power: Base Electron, an independent power producer in which Applied Digital owns approximately 10%, is developing roughly 1.2 GW of front-of-the-meter, on-grid natural gas-fired generation in the Dakotas (collaborating with Babcock & Wilcox and regional utilities); CEO: initial capacity is timed for 2029 and 2030 and then continues to ramp, and Base Electron is working on another project in a different part of North Dakota. The generation goes through the utilities Applied Digital already works with and serves its campuses as well as other retailers on the regional system. CEO: Applied Digital has a lot to build for 2026, 2027 and some 2028, after which additional power capacity (Base Electron plus other regional generation and transmission projects, including a JETx line between Ellendale and Jamestown that will expand Ellendale power capacity) should let it expand all of its campuses, which all go north of a gigawatt. At Polaris Forge 1, use of excess regional grid capacity has returned more than $45 million in electricity credits to local ratepayers.
quarterly_data.figure: Base Electron roughly 1.2 GW gas-fired generation, initial capacity in 2029 and 2030; approximately 10% ownership; more than $45 million electricity credits to local ratepayers
quarterly_data.counterparty_role: independent power producer, approximately 10% owned by Applied Digital

quarterly_data.signal: Demand and customer strategy (CEO): no change in demand from inflationary pressures - pricing is moving higher, and he sees 'extraordinarily robust demand' from both high investment-grade hyperscalers and the next tier. Applied Digital purposely avoided signing leases with the very large model companies, citing volatility in model leadership, and focused on high investment-grade customers, durable contracts and SLAs; leases run at least 15 years and the CEO views the buildings as 30+ year assets. Its AI factories are designed to handle GPUs, TPUs and CPUs and would also work for lower-density standard cloud deployments. It is an approved supplier with every major hyperscaler and replicates each campus with a franchise model of approximately 15 to 20 leadership positions. CEO market view: U.S. technology companies have committed to approximately $850 billion of data center lease obligations over the next several years, up roughly $570 billion year-over-year, and he cites projections of hyperscaler AI infrastructure spending reaching approximately 3.2% of U.S. GDP in 2027.
quarterly_data.figure: approximately $850 billion of data center lease obligations (up roughly $570 billion year-over-year), as cited by the CEO

quarterly_data.signal: ChronoScale (the separated cloud business, trading on Nasdaq as CHRN since early May; Applied Digital holds 96%): Applied Digital consolidated $18.8 million of ChronoScale revenue for the quarter and excludes the segment from its non-GAAP results. During the quarter ChronoScale extended a customer contract at higher pricing for its deployed fleet of GPUs and began demonstrating its secure enterprise AI environment to select partners. CEO: ChronoScale is pursuing multiple large reserve contract opportunities that, if secured on favorable terms, would let it deploy hundreds of megawatts of compute on take-or-pay long-term contracts.
